title: Lecture 4 – Thyrotoxicosis & Graves disease

Source: Curs IV_MG-e-disf tiroidiene 2022 Oct.pptx – 44 slides

HYPERTHYROIDISM (THYROTOXICOSIS) #1

  • HYPOTHYROIDISM
  • Topics

THYROTOXICOSIS & HYPERTHYROIDIDM #2

  • Thyrotoxicosis = the clinical sdr that results when tissues are exposed to high levels of circulating TH
  • Hyperthyroidism = the manifestations result from overproduction of hormone by the thyroid gland itself

Classification of Thyrotoxicosis #3

  • Thyrotoxicosis with Hyperthyroidism
  • Grave’s disease
  • Toxic multinodular goiter
  • Toxic adenoma
  • Iodine-induced (Jod-Basedow)
  • TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma
  • Thyrotoxicosis without Hyperthyroidism (not true hyperthyroidism)
  • Thyrotoxicosis factitious (← iatrogenic or voluntary ingestion of ↑ T4 or TH preparation )
  • Subacute thyroiditis
  • Thyroiditis with transient thyrotoxicosis
  • (silent, postpartum thyroiditis, Hashytoxicosis)
  • Ectopic thyroid tissue (struma ovari )

1. BASEDOW-GRAVES’ DISEASE the most common form of thyrotoxocosis =diffuse goiter, thyrotoxicosis, infiltrative ophtalmophathy +/_ infiltrative dermopathy (5-10%) Is an autoimmune disease of unknown cause • ! There is an underlying genetic predisposition (strong familial predisposition), but it is not clear what “ triggers “the acute episode → A number of interacting susceptibility genes. There is an association with HLA-B8, DR3 and DR2 Some factors that may incite the acute episode : psychological stress, pregnancy, particularly the postpartum period, infection, tobacco use and iodine exposure Pathogenesis : the major atg of Grave’s disease is TSH-Rec T- Ly become sensitized to atgs within the thyroid gland and (+) B-Ly to synthesize antibodies (Abs ) to these antigens; TSHRAbs (Abs directed against the TSH rec- the thyroid cell membrane = TSI )→ thyroid growth, ↑ vascularity, ↑ rate of thyroid hormone production and secretion The natural history of the disease is one of fluctuation, many patients showing a pattern of alternating relapse and remission; perhaps only 40% of subjects have a single episode. Many patients eventually become hypothyroid. #4

2. TOXIC ADENOMA (Plummer’s disease) = a functioning adenoma hypersecreting T3, T4; Pathogenesis: several somatic mutations in the TSH-rec gene → constitutive activation of the TSH rec in the absence of TSH The typical patient is an older individual (usually> 40) tyrotoxicosis + palpable /not palpable thyroid lump The cardiovascular manifestations may be prominent; infiltrative ophatalmopathy or dermopathy are never present!!! Physical examination reveals a definite nodule on one side, with very little thyroid tissue on the other side 3. TOXIC MULTINODULAR GOITER Usually occurs in older patients with long standing euthyroid multinodular goiter; ↑ in the extent of autonomous function→ the disease to move from the nontoxic → to the toxic phase #5

4. IODINE-INDUCED HYPERTHYROIDISM → adm. of pharmacologic doses of iodide containing drugs to subjects with iodine deficiency goiter → in iodine-induced hyperthyroidism (also called the Iod-Basedow phenomenon) and even Grave’s disease Causes :amiodarone ( contains 37% iodine ( ≈75 mg/tb), coronarography , CT urogram, CT ( radiographyc contrast media) Thyrotoxicosis + diffuse or multinodular goiter Confirmation that the patient has been exposed to large quantities of iodine : ↓ RAIU ↑urinary iodine excretion (>several mg/day) Amiodarone-induced THYROTOXICOSIS 2% -USA due to the excess iodine ( also called type 1 amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis); due to an amiodarone-induced thyroiditis, with inflammation and release of stored hormone into the bloodstream ( also termed type 2-amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis). 5. TSH-SECRETING PITUITARY ADENOMA rare goiter + hyperthyroidism #6

6. SUBACUTE Thyroiditis and SILENTor Painless Thyroiditis, POSTPARTUM THYROIDITIS (Hashitoxicosis-autoimmune) mild→ severe thyrotoxicosis, following an acute release of T4, T3 into circulation !!! These illness can be differentiated from others forms of thyrotoxicosis in that RAIU is ↓↓ and the symptoms usually subside spontaneously over a period of weeks or month 7. STRUMA OVARY A teratoma of the ovary contains thyroid tissue that becomes hyperactive ! No goiter or eye signs RAIU over the neck is ↓; total body scan reveals uptake of I131 in the pelvis #7

Slide 8 #8

Clinical features (all forms) #9

  • Effects on – CNS, cardiovascular system, gastrointestinal tube , neuromuscular system, lipid, protein, carbohydrate metabolisms
  • 1.GENERAL MANIFESTATIONS :↑ basal metabolic rate and sometimes slightly elevated basal body temperature ( 37-37.5°C), heat intolerance, sweating
  • 2. Nervous system
  • Alterations in NS function are manifested by:
  • Emotional lability, nervousness, irritability
  • Insomnia, restlessness, shortness of attention span
  • Fine, rhythmic tremor of the hands, tongue, or slightly closed eyelids
  • Hyperkinesia,hyperreflexia
  • 3. CARDIOVASCULAR SYSTEM
  • ↑ cardiac output and ↑↑ in heart rate in hyperthyroidism  the most common complaints: palpitations
  • tachycardia is almost always present.
  • functional systolic murmurs
  • cardiac arrhythmias are almost invariably supraventricular (extrasystoles, atrial fibrillation, paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, )
  • widening of pulse pressure ←( ↑ systolic BP ← ↑cardiac output; ↓ diastolic pressure  ↓ peripheral vascular resistance )
  • hyperkinetic cardiovascular syndrome; congestive (high output) heart failure

Clinical features #10

  • 4. DIGESTIVE MANIFESTATIONS
  • An ↑ in appetite but with weight loss
  • ↑ gut motility ( stools are frequently soft , but diarrhea is rare)
  • Hepatic dysfunction occurs, particularly when thyrotoxicosis is severe
  • 5. MUSCULAR EFFECTS
  • Weakness and fatigability ; weakness is most prominent in the proximal muscles of limbs, causing difficulty in climbing stairs ( “ chair sign”)
  • 6. ENDOCRINE manifestation
  • ♀: Menstrual abnormalities: ovulation may be impaired, oligomenorrhea, secondary amenorrhea
  • In ♂: erectile dysfunction, gynecomastia
  • 7 .SKIN and HAIR
  • - warm, moist, pink skin; excessive sweating; the patient blushes readily
  • - the hair is fine and friable and hair loss may be excessive; the nails are often soft and friable

Clinical manifestations #11

  • 8. EYES
  • retraction of the upper or lower eyelids, or both, evident as the presence of a rim of sclera between either lid and the limbus, may be seen in all forms of thyrotoxicosis; responsible for the typical stare of the patient
  • lid lag
  • globe lag
  • A fine tremor of the lightly closed lids can often be observed= Rosenbach’ s sign
  • = Class 1 (O) of the Werner’s classification of eye signs in Graves’ disease
  • ! These ocular manifestations appear to be the result of ↑ adrenergic activity. (will often abate when the thyrotoxicosis is relieved)
  • !!!! It is important to differentiate these ocular manifestations (=class 1(0) of Werner’s classification), which occur in all forms of thyrotoxicosis, from those of infiltrative orbitopathy, which are characteristic of hyperthyroid Graves’ disease.

Manifestations of Graves’s disease (in addition to those common to all forms of thyrotoxicosis, presented before) Goiter Graves’ disease– the goiter is diffuse and usual symmetrical; the consistency varies from soft to firm and rubbery; the surface is generally smooth; in severe cases, a thrill may be felt, and a thrill is always accompanied by an audible bruit ( the thrills and bruits  ↑ blood flow) #12

Manifestations of Graves’s disease INFILTRATIVE ORBITOPATHY of GRAVES’DISEASE (THYROID-ASSOCIATED OPHTALMOPATHY or ORBITOPATHY)(TAO) precedes, follows or its onset is simultaneous with thyrotoxic manifestations More frequently in women More severe in men bi/unilateral, symmetrical / asymmetrical !!! Smoking cigarettes –potential risk factor for the development of TAO Clinic irritation in the eyes, excessive tearing that is often made worse by exposure to air or wind, periorbital edema, photophobia, chemosis, scleral injection, retrobulbar pressure or pain, extraocular muscle dysfunction: double vision exophthalmos (proptosis:Upper limits of normal according to race- white: 20 mm; Asian: 18 mm; black: 22 mm (as measured by the Hertel exophthalmometer) + exposure keratitis, optic neuropathy; #13

WERNER’S CLASSIFICATION OF EYE CHANGES IN GRAVE’S DISEASE The mnemonic -”NOSPECS”- class 0 (N) : no signs or symptoms class 1 (O) – only signs, no symptoms ( signs limited to upper lid retraction, stare, lid lag, globe lag…) class 2 (S) :soft tissue involvement: periorbital edema, irritation in the eyes, excesive tearing, conjunctival congestion or edema (chemosis), enlarged lacrimal glands ; proptosis <22mm Class 3 (P): proptosis >=22mm Class 4 (E)– extraocular muscle involvement ( most commonly inferior rectus, medial rectus)diplopia; ophthalmoplegia (especially of upward gaze← affection of the inferior rectus); convergence defect caused by infiltrative, fibrotic contraction of the medial rectus Class 5 (C) – corneal involvement (keratitis) due to inability to close the eyes completely =lagophthalmos (usually, proptosis >32mm), Class 6 (S) – sight loss (optic nerve involvement) ← likely due to ischemia of the nerve from compression of the surrounding enlarged extraocular muscles !Classes 2-6 represents true infiltrative disease involving orbital muscle and orbital tissues and are specific to Graves’ disease. #14

Rare #15

  • -thickening of the skin, particularly over the
  • lower tibia or on the dorsum of the feet, with a peau d’orange surface (hyperpigmented,
  • nonpitting induration of the skin).
  • Manifestations of Graves’s disease
  • INFILTRATIVE DERMOPATHY (PRETIBIL MYXEDEMA)
  • Thyroid acropachy
  • is very rare and consists of clubbing, swollen fingers and periosteal
  • new bone formation.

Conditions associated with Graves’s disease #16

  • DM Type 1
  • CSR I
  • vitiligo, celiac disease, myasthenia gravis

Investigation of thyrotoxicosis #17

  • 1. HORMONAL ASSESSEMENT
  • TSH/↓↓,  FT4 (+FT3)
  • exception: TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma: ↑ TSH, FT4↑
  • 2. IMAGISTIC INVESTIGATIONS
  • Thyroid ultrasonography
  • Graves’ disease – diffuse thyroid hypertrophy, with an homogenous, hypoechoic aspect
  • Toxic adenoma/toxic multinodular goiter– one nodule/ enlarged gland that is diffusely inhomogeneous with multiple individual nodules
  • RAIU (+ isotope scanning)-employed if diagnosis is doubtful, but are seldom required
  • ↑ RAIU: in thyrotoxicosis with hyperthyroidism: Graves disease, toxic adenoma, toxic multinodular goiter
  • ↓ RAIU: in subacute thyroiditis or “ silent thyroiditis”, iodine-induced hyperthyroidism
  • THYROID SCINTHYGRAPHY ( RADIOIODINE SCAN)- very rarely used
  • Graves’disease – enlarged gland that is usually rather symmetric with a typically very homogenous distribution of tracer
  • Toxic adenoma – a “ hot “ nodule with ↓ or absent function of the contralateral lobe
  • Toxic multinodular goiter – multiple functioning nodules in the gland or occasionally an irregular, patchy distribution of radioactive iodine

TRAbs(+) –are highly specific to Graves’ disease (human autoimmune thyroid disease) useful in patients who presents with unilateral or bilateral exophtalmos without obvious signs or laboratory manifestations of Graves’ disease; useful indicator of the degree of disease activity and the level of TRAbs correlates with the severity of the eye disease also useful in the assessment of cessation of carbimazole (persisting ↑titres predicts recurrence) and in pregnant women to assess the risk of fetal thyrotoxicosis. TPO Abs and TG Abs are usually present in both Graves’ disease and Hashimoto’s thyroiditis 3. OTHERS glycaemia normal/↑, IGT, DM   cholesterol n/  AF ECG – sinus tachycardia, AF, SVT, LVH #18

  • ULTRASONOGRAPHY, CT and MRI scan of the orbits : reveal extraocular muscle enlargement in most patients with Graves’ disease

Complications #19

  • THYROTOXIC CRISIS (“ THYROID STORM”)
  • = the acute exacerbation of all of the symptoms and signs of thyrotoxicosis; life-threatening
  • Fever (38-41ºC), cardiac arrhythmias , heart failure, diarrhea, vomiting, marked agitation, delirium, coma
  • THYROTOXIC CARDIAC INVOLVEMENT (CARDIOTHYREOSIS)
  • cardiac arrhythymias– AF
  • Heart failure
  • Myocardial ischemia
  • THYROTOXIC MYOPATHY
  • In severe untreated cases, muscle wasting (proximal) develops out of proportion = thyrotoxic myopathy
  • THYROTOXIC OSTEOPOROSIS
  • DIABETES MELLITUS
  • THYROTOXIC HEPATHOPATHY
  • Hepatic dysfunction occurs particularly when thyrotoxicosis is severe – jaundice, hepatomegaly, ↑ ALT

TREATMENT OF HYPERTHYROIDISM #20

  • Objectives:
  • To induce remission in Graves’ disease
  • Monitor for relapse off treatment on a regular basis
  • Methods of treatment;
  • 1. Medical treatment- Antithyroid drug therapy
  • 2. Surgery
  • 3. Radioactive iodine therapy

TREATMENT OF HYPERTHYROIDISM #21

  • Medical treatment
  • Antithyroid drugs (ATS)
  • Mechanisms of action: ( - ) TPO-mediated iodination of Tg to form T4,T3 within the thyroid gland
  • I. IMIDAZOLE DERIVATES
  • TIAMAZOLE (THYROZOL) 5mg/tb
  • CARBIMAZOLE 5mg/tb, METHYMAZOLE
  • II. THIOURACIL DERIVATES
  • METYLTHIOURACIL (50 mg/tb)
  • PROPYLTHIOURACIL (PTU)(50 mg/tb)
  • PTU (but not methimazole ) blocks also peripheral T4  T3 conversion ( =advantage in severe thyrotoxicosis)
  • both drugs may have immunosuppressive effects that may be responsible for the remission from the disease that some patients have after 1-2 years of treatment ;
  • Initial dose - larger dose ( 30-40 mg/ day of thyrozol )
  • Maintenance dose- 5-10 mg/day
  • SE : rash, agranulocytosis(= indication for discontinuing the medication),
  • cholestatic jaundice with tiamazole and hepatocellular toxicity with PTU (!!! PTU should not be used as a first-line agent),
  • - PTU = preferred in pregnant women (1st trim)

TREATMENT OF HYPERTHYROIDISM #22

  • Surgical treatment
  • Indications:
  • a) Relapse of Graves’ disease
  • b) Very large, compressive glands, multinodular goiters
  • c) Patients who are allergic to or noncompliant with ATD,
  • d) Patients who refuse radioactive iodine
  • e) Documented suspicious or malignant thyroid nodule by FNAB.
  • Total thyroidectomy is now considered the operation of choice
  • Thyroidectomy should be performed only in patients who have previously been rendered euthyroid.
  • The patient is prepared with ATD until euthyroid; in addition, starting 2 weeks before the day of operation, saturated solution of potassium iodide (SSKI) or Lugol’s solution (3* 3drops daily → 3* 15 drops/day ) is added  will diminish the hyperplasia and hypervascularity of the gland (the gland usually becomes firm) and simplify surgery
  • ! Complications of surgery: hypothyroidism, hypoparathyroidism, recurrent laryngeal nerve injury

Radioactive iodine therapy =the preferred treatment for most patients over age 21 (in US) Indications: a) Definitive treatment of multinodular goiter or adenoma. b) Relapsed Graves’s disease c) Allergy to ATD d) Contraindications to surgery 3-10 mCi 131I Following the administration of radioactive iodine (which typically is giving orally as a single capsule) the gland will shrink and the patient will usually become euthyroid over a period of 2-6 months SE : Hypothyroidism is the almost inevitable complication of radioactive iodine therapy ( > 80%) – Radioiodine can exacerbate eye problems and may even induce mild eye disease in those without eye disease however, potential worsening can be prevented by administration of prednisone 40-60mg/day for 1-2 months (gradually tapering the dose) following the radioiodine treatment Contraindications: Young children because of the potential risk of thyroid carcinogenesis. Severe ophtalmopathy Pregnant and lactating ♀ #23

Treatment of hyperthyroidism #24

  • Other medical measures
  • Rest
  • Beta-adrenergic blocking agents : propranolol
  • 10-40mgevery 6 hours or longer acting beta-blockers : metoprolol, atenolol control many adrenergic symptoms, tachycardia, hypertension
  • Sedatives
  • multivitamins

Medical treatment of infiltrative orbitopathy #25

  • If the patient is thyrotoxic, this should be treated/hypothyroidism must be avoided
  • Stop smoking !!!
  • Symptomatic treatment : ( useful mainly in mild forms) dark glasses ( for those with photophobia, sensitivity to wind or cold air), artificial tears
  • Selenium may improve symptoms in patients with mild Graves’s ophthalmopathy (100 micrograms bd)
  • Glucocorticoids :
  • Intravenous methylprednisolone ( 500 mg/week for 6 weeks followed by 250 mg/week for another 6 weeks) in moderate-severe forms- (cumulative dose of 4.5 g) or
  • the high-dose regimen(= a starting dose of 0.75 g i.v. methylprednisolone once weekly for 6 weeks, followed by 0.5 g once weekly for 6 weeks, cumulative dose 7.5 g) in very severe cases
  • → the advantage of fewer SE than with high doses of prednisone) OR
  • Prednisone 50-60mg/day, tapering the dose 10mg every 2 weeks
  • Alternatives: Mycophenolate / Cyclosporine/(as monotherapy and in combination with i.v./oral glucocorticoids
  • External radiation to the retrobulbar area
  • The dosage is usually: 1000 cGy/ orbit in 10 fractions given over a period of 10 days
  • → if corticosteroid therapy is not effective or contraindicated
  • The best results are obtained by combining these 2 therapies ( glucocorticoids + external x-ray therapy)

Surgical treatment of infiltrative orbitopathy #26

  • Surgical orbital decompression may be required, particularly in very severe cases, if pressure of orbital contents on the optic nerve threatens vision (often called a ‘hot’ decompression) or at a later, stable stage for cosmetic reasons (‘cold’ decompression).
  • Surgery for strabismus (after any necessary orbital decompression and when eyes are in a quiescent phase for at least 6 months after active disease)
  • → aims to allow correct binocular vision
  • Eyelid surgery
  • -will protect the cornea if lids cannot be closed, and can be useful later for cosmetic reasons.

HYPOTHYROIDISM #27

Hypothyroidism #28

  • = a clinical syndrome resulting from a deficiency of thyroid hormones, which in turn results in a generalized slowing down of metabolic processes
  • Myxedema
  • Classification:
  • – according to etiology;
  • Primary (thyroid failure)-by far the most common
  • Central (due to pituitary TSH deficiency or hypothalamic deficiency of TRH)
  • Peripheral resistance to the action of TH

Etiology of primary hypothyroidism #29

  •  Primary hypothyroidism with goiter
  • 1. CONGENITAL
  • Inherited defects in hormone biosynthesis (thyroid dyshormonogenesis) (e.g. Pendred sdr (← mutations in the pendrin gene)= a defect in iodine organification+ sensory nerve deafness)
  • Endemic cretinism
  • 2. ACQUIRED
  • Hashimoto’s thyroiditis=by far the most common cause
  • Excessive iodide intake (radiocontrast dye, amiodarone)
  • Severe iodine deficiency (endemic goiter)- very rare
  • Cytokines: interferon alfa (used to treat hepatitis C)
  •  Primary hypothyroidism (atrophic)
  • 1. CONGENITAL
  •  Thyroid agenesis
  •  Ectopic thyroid( lingual thyroid)-functions poorly ( absence of thyroid tissue or its ectopic location can be ascertained by scintiscanning!)
  • 2. ACQUIRED
  •  Hashimoto’s disease
  •  Postablative due to 131 I (radioactive iodine therapy), surgery
  •  Transient (Post-thyroiditis ) hypothyroidism
  • Subacute thyroiditis
  • Postpartum, silent thyroiditis

Clinical Presentations and Findings #30

  • Newborn Infants (Cretinism) / Endemic Cretinism
  • Severe hypothyroidism in infants is termed cretinism.
  • retardation of mental development and
  • retardation of growth
  • = are the hallmark of cretinism or congenital hypothyroidism.
  • There is an inverse relationship between age at diagnosis and intelligence quotient (IQ) in later life.
  • Congenital hypothyroidism- possible causes:
  • inherited defects in thyroid hormone biosynthesis,
  • absent or ectopic thyroid gland that functions poorly
  • → sporadic congenital hypothyriodism (sporadic cretinism) ( commonly seen in the Western world). There is no association with iodine deficiency
  • severe iodine deficiency,
  • Endemic cretinism is defined by three major criteria:
  • It has a strong epidemiologic association with endemic goitre and severe iodine deficiency.
  • Its clinical features comprise mental developmental disability, together with either a neurological syndrome or a syndrome of hypothyroidism and stunted growth.
  •  mental retardation, a characteristic puffy appearance of the face and hands, deaf mutism, motor spasticity, gait disturbance etc

Congenital iodine deficiency sdr #31

  • Features of congenital hypothyroidism
  • +
  • • Physiological jaundice.
  • • Goitre.
  • • Hoarse cry, feeding problems, constipation, somnolence.
  • • Delay in reaching normal milestones of development, short stature with the limbs disproportionately short in relation to the trunk.
  • • Impaired mental development, retarded bone age.
  • • Epiphyseal dysgenesis, delayed dentition.

Slide 32 #32

  • !!! Early diagnosis and treatment of congenital hypothyroidism are essential because it can prevent permanent retardation, cerebral damage
  • The treatment is simple, effective, and
  • Inexpensive (= consists of a daily dose of thyroid hormone (thyroxine) by mouth, irrespective of the cause of congenital hypothyroidism)
  • →nearly all of the developed world
  • practices routine newborn screening for TSH or T4
  • (24-48 h after birth) to detect and treat
  • congenital hypothyroidism in the first weeks of life.
  • !!! Iodine deficiency is the most common preventable cause of brain damage worldwide.

Clinical Presentations and Findings #33

  • Children and Adolescents
  • Hypothyroidism in children and adolescents is characterized by:
  • retarded growth and short stature,
  • the typical signs and symptoms of hypothyroidism seen in adults (see later), and
  • variable but usually declining school performance.
  • delayed/precocious puberty may occur
  • Adults
  • - in severe cases the clinical presentation of MYXEDEMA.

Clinical features- ADULTHOOD #34

  • Insidious onset
  • The common features of moderate- severe hypothyroidism include:
  • Fatigability
  • Central and peripheral NS :all intellectual functions, including speech (thick, slurred speech, hoarseness) are slowed; loss of initiative, memory deficits, lethargy and somnolence; psychiatric disorders are common: depression or even agitation (“myxedema madness”) ; slow reflexes
  • Hearing loss
  • Digestive manifestations
  • Constipation,
  • ↓appetite,
  • Modest gain in weight (generally <10-20pounds(4.5-9 kg))
  • Neuromuscular system: numbness and tingling of the extremities, muscle cramps, muscle weakness; cold sensitivity

Skin and appendages: #35

  • cool, rough, dry, pale skin; puffy face, hands and feet ( ←non-pitting edema)→ ”pale moon-like face” or “”toad-like face”; ↓ conversion of carotene to vit A may give the skin a yellowish color;
  • hair may be lost from the temporal aspects of the eyebrows=Herthoge’s sign;
  • head and body hair is dry and brittle and tends to fall out

Clinical features #36

  • Cardiovascular signs
  • → impaired ventricular contraction, bradycardia, ↑peripheral resistance resulting in ↓cardiac output, narrowing of pulse pressure
  • convergent BP formula (dBP=90-100mm Hg ←↑ systemic vascular resistance) ; heart sounds are diminished in intensity
  • Cardiac enlargement ← interstitial edema, left ventricular dilatation, (nonhemodynamically significant) pericardial effusion
  • Reproductive function
  • Excessive menstrual bleeding , menorrhagia , failure of ovulation, ↓fertility, galactorrhea
  • ↓libido, impotence, oligospermia

Clinical features #37

  • Hashimoto’s thyroiditis may associate other autoimmune disorders
  • Endocrine
  • CSRI (with adrenal autoantibodies), gonadal insufficiency , DM type I (with islet cell antibodies0
  • Non-endocrine
  • vitiligo, pernicious anemia, alopecia
  • These conditions are part of what has been termed “autoimmune polyglandular syndrome” type 1 or 2 (Schmidt’s syndrome)

HYPOTHYROIDISM-Diagnosis #38

  • 1. Hormonal determinations
  • Primary Hypothyroidism – the combination of TSH + (FT4)=diagnostic
  • Central Hypothyroidism – TSH/low-normal, FT4 
  • 2. Anti-Tg antibodies, anti-TPO antibodies =↑ in Hashimoto’s thyroiditis
  • 3. Additional laboratory and imagistic investigations
  • ECG reveals low-voltage of QRS complexes and P and T waves; prolongation of the QT and PR intervals, sinus bradycardia; rarely complete heart block; alterations of the ST segment and flattened or inverted T waves
  • Thoracic X-ray may reveal cardiac enlargement.
  • Echocardiography is useful in detecting the pericardial effusion.

Laboratory investigations #39

  • Biochemical tests
  • -creatinine kinase, LDH, AST, ALT are often raised
  • -the lipid profile =altered with ↑ LDL cholesterol and ↑ triglycerides
  • In a hypothyroid patient, hyponatraemia ← ↓ renal tubular water loss or, less commonly, due to coexisting cortisol deficiency.
  • Haematological tests
  • Anemia: ←there are a few mechanisms that may contribute to anemia:
  •  a macrocytosis is typical ←folate deficiency from impaired intestinal absorption of folic acid, although concurrent vitamin B12 deficiency should be considered.
  •  microcytic hypochromic anaemia due to menorrhagia and impaired iron utilization (impaired intestinal absorption of iron)
  •  mild normocytic, normochromic anemia ← impaired hemoglobin synthesis
  • Endocrine tests
  • Serum prolactin may be elevated because ↑TRH leads to ↑prolactin secretion (may be partly responsible for ↓fertility in young women with hypothyroidism).

A 63-year-old man with Hashimoto thyroiditis. #40

  • Longitudinal scan shows hypoechoic, slightly heterogeneous left lobe (arrows).
  • A 49-year-old woman with Graves’ disease.
  • Transverse scan shows an enlarged hypoechoic thyroid gland.
  • Thyroid ultrasonography – thyroid volume: normal, ↑, ↓;
  • in Hashimoto’s thyroiditis: an hypoechoic aspect is usually present

Slide 41 #41

  • Technetium scan: Left-sided hemiagenesis of the thyroid lobe. The left lobe was not visualized on USG and the 12-year-old teenager had hypothyroidism (TSH = 12 µUi/ml, FT4= 12 pmol/l)
  • RAIU + Thyroid scintigraphy – usually employed ONLY for assessing:
  • inherited defects in hormone biosynthesis or
  • thyroid agenesis, ectopic thyroid gland
  • Thyroid scintigraphy showing the ectopic lingual thyroid.
  • Tumor at the base of the tongue of the submucosal aspect.

Complications #42

  • 1.Myxedema coma: the end stage of untreated hypothyroidism; it is characterized by progressive weakness, stupor, hypothermia (T< 35 ºC), hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hypoventilation and it may ultimately result in shock and death
  • 2. Myxedema cardiomyopathy → congestive heart failure
  • ECG – bradycardia, prolongation of the QT and PR intervals, AV block
  • Echocardiography – cardiac hypertrophy, then ventricular enlargement with  EF
  • 3. Myxedema pericarditis ( pericardial effusion is rarely of sufficient magnitude to cause tamponade)
  • 4. Coronary artery disease- likely related to ↑ levels of total cholesterol, LDL-cholesterol
  • 5. Myopathy
  • 6. In newborn infants – impairment of linear growth results in dwarfism +retardation of mental and physical development

Treatment of Hypothyroidism #43

  • = Thyroid hormone replacement with synthetic levothyroxine remains the treatment of choice.
  • Drugs
  • L-T4 (Levothyroxine, Euthyrox) 50-100(200)microg/day with a mean of 125 µg/day
  • the T1/2 of T4 is about 7days, so it need be given only once daily; before breakfast for an optimal absorption
  • ( L-T4/T3 (NOVOTHYRAL) 100 LT4 + 20T3/tb)
  • Considerations:
  • Usually for life, with the exception of transient hypothyroidism (e.g. subacute thyroiditis);
  • The initial dose of levothyroxine prescribed depends on the degree of hypothyroidism, the age and general health of the patient
  • in most patients (young or middle- aged and otherwise healthy with no associated cardiovascular or other abnormalities ), one can begin treatment with the full estimated dose requirement
  • in older patients or patients with underlying heart disease, it is best to start with a low dose of T4 (eg 25 µg/day) and increase the dose slowly( at 1-2 week intervals) until the full dose required with careful clinical and laboratory evaluation ; association of beta-adrenergic blocking agents is helpful

Treatment of Hypothyroidism #44

  • Optimum dose is determined by clinical criteria
  • The goal in primary hypothyroidism
  • to restore serum TSH concentrations to the normal range.
  • the serum TSH should be evaluated 6 weeks after a theoretically completed replacement dose has been instituted
  • In central hypothyroidism
  • - serum FT4 should be restored to a concentration in the upper half of the normal range.
  • ! such patients should also be evaluated and treated for glucocorticoid deficiency before institution of thyroid replacement
  • Monitoring replacement therapy: initially at 6-8weeks, then 2*/year
